name: BlackByte
summary: BlackByte is a ransomware threat actor operating since at least 2021. BlackByte is associated with several versions of ransomware also labeled BlackByte Ransomware. BlackByte ransomware operations initially used a common encryption key allowing for the development of a universal decryptor, but subsequent versions such as BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware use more robust encryption mechanisms. BlackByte is notable for operations targeting critical infrastructure entities among other targets across North America.

procedures.text: BlackByte staged encryption keys on virtual private servers operated by the adversary.
BlackByte has staged tools such as Cobalt Strike at public file sharing and hosting sites.
BlackByte captured credentials for or impersonated domain administration users.
BlackByte has gained access to victim environments through legitimate VPN credentials.
BlackByte exploited vulnerabilities such as ProxyLogon and ProxyShell for initial access to victim environments.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use known credentials to run commands and spawn processes as a local user account.
BlackByte created malicious services for ransomware execution.
BlackByte used WMI to delete Volume Shadow Copies on victim machines.
BlackByte created scheduled tasks for payload execution.
BlackByte used encoded PowerShell commands during operations. BlackByte has used remote PowerShell commands in victim networks.
BlackByte executed ransomware using the Windows command shell.
BlackByte Ransomware: BlackByte Ransomware uses the `SetThreadExecutionState` API to prevent the victim system from entering sleep.
BlackByte Ransomware: BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as a JavaScript launcher file.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use VBA to perform execution.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use Python to perform execution.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can download a hosted "beacon" payload using BITSAdmin.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can exploit Oracle Java vulnerabilities for execution, including CVE-2011-3544, CVE-2013-2465, CVE-2012-4681, and CVE-2013-2460.
BlackByte performed Registry modifications to escalate privileges and disable security tools.
BlackByte modified multiple services on victim machines to enable encryption operations. BlackByte has installed tools such as AnyDesk as a service on victim machines.
BlackByte created privileged domain accounts during intrusions.
BlackByte has used ASPX web shells following exploitation of vulnerabilities in services such as Microsoft Exchange.
BlackByte has used Registry Run keys for persistence.

Mimikatz: The Mimikatz credential dumper has been extended to include Skeleton Key domain controller authentication bypass functionality. The `LSADUMP::ChangeNTLM` and `LSADUMP::SetNTLM` modules can also manipulate the password hash of an account without knowing the clear text value.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike has the ability to use an Excel Workbook to execute additional code by enabling Office to trust macros and execute code without user permission.
Mimikatz: The Mimikatz credential dumper contains an implementation of an SSP.
BlackByte has injected Cobalt Strike into `wuauclt.exe` during intrusions. BlackByte has injected ransomware into `svchost.exe` before encryption.
BlackByte has exploited CVE-2024-37085 in VMWare ESXi software for authentication bypass and subsequent privilege escalation.
BlackByte used process hollowing for defense evasion purposes.
BlackByte constructed a valid authentication token following Microsoft Exchange exploitation to allow for follow-on privileged command execution.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike has the ability to load DLLs via reflective injection.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can steal access tokens from exiting processes.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can spawn processes with alternate PPIDs.

Mimikatz: Mimikatz's `MISC::AddSid` module can append any SID or user/group account to a user's SID-History. Mimikatz also utilizes SID-History Injection to expand the scope of other components such as generated Kerberos Golden Tickets and DCSync beyond a single domain.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use a number of known techniques to bypass Windows UAC.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use `sudo` to run a command.
BlackByte has encoded commands in base64-encoded sections concatenated together in PowerShell. BlackByte uses PowerShell commands to disable Windows Defender.
BlackByte deleted ransomware executables post-encryption.

BlackByte stopped execution if identified language settings on victim machines was Russian or one of several language associated with former Soviet republics. BlackByte has used ransomware variants requiring a key passed on the command line for the malware to execute.
BlackByte masqueraded configuration files containing encryption keys as PNG files.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware: BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware can timestomp files for defense evasion and anti-forensics purposes.
BlackByte Ransomware: BlackByte Ransomware checks for files related to known sandboxes.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can hash functions to obfuscate calls to the Windows API and use a public/private key pair to encrypt Beacon session metadata.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike includes a capability to modify the Beacon payload to eliminate known signatures or unpacking methods.
BlackByte Ransomware: BlackByte Ransomware is distributed as an encrypted payload.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use `rundll32.exe` to load DLL from the command line.
Cobalt Strike: The Cobalt Strike loader can use the `MessageBoxA` API to prompt for user interaction as an anti-sandbox measure.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use spoof arguments in spawned processes that execute beacon commands.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike's `execute-assembly` command can run a.NET executable within the memory of a sacrificial process by loading the CLR.
BlackByte disabled security tools such as Windows Defender and the Raccine anti-ransomware tool during operations.
BlackByte modified firewall rules on victim machines to enable remote system discovery.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz’s `LSADUMP::DCShadow` module can be used to make AD updates by temporarily setting a computer to be a DC.

BlackByte Ransomware: BlackByte Ransomware uses the `mountvol.exe` command to mount volume names and leverages the Microsoft Discretionary Access Control List tool, `icacls.exe`, to grant the group to “Everyone” full access to the root of the drive.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use self signed Java applets to execute signed applet attacks.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware: BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware modifies the Windows firewall during execution.
BlackByte Ransomware: BlackByte Ransomware enables SMBv1 during execution.
BlackByte used tools such as Cobalt Strike and Mimikatz to dump credentials from victim systems.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can spawn a job to inject into LSASS memory and dump password hashes.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can recover hashed passwords.

Mimikatz: Mimikatz performs credential dumping to obtain account and password information useful in gaining access to additional systems and enterprise network resources. It contains functionality to acquire information about credentials in many ways, including from the LSA.

procedures.text: Mimikatz: Mimikatz contains functionality to acquire credentials from the Windows Credential Manager.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz's kerberos module can create golden tickets.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz's kerberos module can create silver tickets.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz's `CRYPTO` module can create and export various types of authentication certificates.
BlackByte used tools such as Arp to pull system network information and identify connected devices.
BlackByte used tools such as Arp to identify remotely-connected devices.
BlackByte enumerated network shares on victim devices.
BlackByte queried registry values to determine system language settings.
BlackByte has used tools such as NetScan to enumerate network services in victim environments.
BlackByte has used tools such as AdFind to identify and enumerate domain accounts.
BlackByte enumerated installed security products during operations.
BlackByte used various system commands and tools to pull system information during operations.
BlackByte enumerated Active Directory information and trust relationships during operations.
BlackByte identified system language settings to determine follow-on execution.
Exbyte: Exbyte checks whether the process is running with privileged local access during execution.
AdFind: AdFind can enumerate domain groups.

procedures.text: Exbyte: Exbyte enumerates all document files on an infected machine, then creates a summary of these items including filename and directory location prior to exfiltration to cloud hosting services.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can enumerate services on compromised hosts.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can produce a sessions report from compromised hosts.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload can collect information on process details.
Cobalt Strike: The Cobalt Strike System Profiler can discover applications through the browser and identify the version of Java the target has.
BlackByte used SMB file shares to distribute payloads throughout victim networks, including BlackByte ransomware variants during wormable operations.
BlackByte transfered tools such as Cobalt Strike and the AnyDesk remote access tool during operations using SMB shares.
BlackByte has used RDP to access other hosts within victim networks.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can perform pass the hash.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can deliver Beacon payloads for lateral movement by leveraging remote COM execution.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can SSH to a remote service.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use `WinRM` to execute a payload on a remote host.
Mimikatz: Mimikatz’s `LSADUMP::DCSync` and `KERBEROS::PTT` modules implement the three steps required to extract the krbtgt account hash and create/use Kerberos tickets.
BlackByte compressed data collected from victim environments prior to exfiltration.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can collect data from a local system.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike's Beacon payload is capable of capturing screenshots.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can perform browser pivoting and inject into a user's browser to inherit cookies, authenticated HTTP sessions, and client SSL certificates.
BlackByte collected victim device information then transmitted this via HTTP POST to command and control infrastructure.
BlackByte has transferred tools such as Cobalt Strike to victim environments from file sharing and hosting websites.
BlackByte has used tools such as AnyDesk in victim environments.

Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can leverage the HTTP protocol for C2 communication, while hiding the actual data in either an HTTP header, URI parameter, the transaction body, or appending it to the URI. Cobalt Strike
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can conduct peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use a custom command and control protocol that can be encapsulated in DNS. All protocols use their standard assigned ports.

Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can be configured to have commands relayed over a peer-to-peer network of infected hosts. This can be used to limit the number of egress points, or provide access to a host without direct internet access.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike has the ability to accept a value for HTTP Host Header to enable domain fronting.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can be configured to use TCP, ICMP, and UDP for C2 communications.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use Base64, URL-safe Base64, or NetBIOS encoding in its C2 traffic.

Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike uses a custom command and control protocol that is encapsulated in HTTP, HTTPS, or DNS. In addition, it conducts peer-to-peer communication over Windows named pipes encapsulated in the SMB protocol. All protocols use their standard assigned ports.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike has the ability to use AES-256 symmetric encryption in CBC mode with HMAC-SHA-256 to encrypt task commands and XOR to encrypt shell code and configuration data.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can use RSA asymmetric encryption with PKCS1 padding to encrypt data sent to the C2 server.
BlackByte has used services such as `anonymfiles.com` and `file.io` to exfiltrate victim data.
BlackByte transmitted collected victim host information via HTTP POST to command and control infrastructure.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike can set its Beacon payload to reach out to the C2 server on an arbitrary and random interval.
Cobalt Strike: Cobalt Strike will break large data sets into smaller chunks for exfiltration.
BlackByte has encrypted victim files for ransom. Early versions of BlackByte ransomware used a common key for encryption, but later versions use unique keys per victim.
BlackByte resized and deleted volume shadow copy files to prevent system recovery after encryption.
BlackByte left ransom notes in all directories where encryption takes place.
BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware: BlackByte 2.0 Ransomware can terminate running services.
